Take a step back from the rack and place your feet in a medium stance, shoulder width apart. Keep your head up the whole time, because looking down throws you off balance, and keep your back straight. That is your starting position.
With your legs held still, inhale and bend at the hips to bring your torso forward. Go down until your torso is parallel to the floor.
Exhale and bring the bar up again by raising your torso to the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Stomach_Vacuum: Stand upright with your feet shoulder width apart and put your hands on your hips. That is your starting position.
Slowly take in as much air as you can. Then breathe out as far as you can, pull your stomach in as far as it goes and stay there. Picture your navel reaching your spine.
A single isometric contraction lasts about 20 seconds. Try to breathe normally through those 20 seconds. Then inhale and let your stomach go back to the starting position.
When you have had some practice, aim to hold for more than 20 seconds. Tip: Build up step by step to 40-60 seconds.
Do as many sets as your plan calls for.
Straight-Arm_Dumbbell_Pullover: Stand a dumbbell upright on a flat bench.

Make sure the dumbbell sits securely on top of the bench. Then lie across the bench at a right angle to it, so that your torso and the bench form a cross and only your shoulders rest on the pad. Your hips are lower than the bench, your legs bent, your feet planted firmly on the floor. Your head hangs off the bench too.

Take the dumbbell in both hands and hold it with straight arms directly above your chest. Both palms press against the underside of one of the dumbbell's ends. That is your starting position. Caution: Always check that the dumbbell you use here is secure. If the plates are loose, the dumbbell can come apart and land on your face.
With straight arms, inhale and slowly lower the weight in an arc behind your head until your chest stretches.
From there, exhale and move the dumbbell back to the starting position along the same arc you lowered it on.
Hold the weight for a second in the starting position, then repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.
Straight-Arm_Pulldown: Take the wide bar on the top pulley of a pulldown machine with a pronated grip, palms down, wider than your shoulders. Then step back about two feet.

Lean your torso forward from the waist by about 30 degrees. Your arms are fully extended in front of you, elbows slightly bent. If your arms are not fully extended, step back a little more until they are. With your arms extended and your torso leaning slightly from the waist, tense your lats; now you are ready to start.
Keep your arms straight and contract your lats to pull the bar down until your hands are beside your thighs. Exhale during this part.
With your arms still straight, inhale and return to the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Straight_Bar_Bench_Mid_Rows: Lay a loaded barbell across the end of a bench. Stand on the bench behind the bar and grip it pronated at medium width. Push your hips back, lift your chest and keep your spine neutral. That is your starting position.
Draw your shoulder blades back and bend your elbows to row the bar up to your torso. Move with control and do not jerk.
Pause briefly, then lower the bar slowly to the starting position and make sure you go down all the way.
Straight_Raises_on_Incline_Bench: Behind the head of an incline bench, lay a bar on the ground.
Lie face down on the bench. Take the barbell off the floor with a pronated grip and straight arms, and let it hang straight down. That is your starting position.
Start by lifting the barbell forward, out in front of your head, with your arms still extended.
Go back to the starting position.
Stride_Jump_Crossover: Stand beside a box and put the foot nearer to it on top, close to the edge.
Start by swinging your arms up and pushing off the upper leg to jump as high as you can. Try to drive the other knee upward.
Land on the other side of the box, in the mirror image of your starting stance: the foot that began on the box is now on the floor and the other foot is on the box.
Do it again, this time crossing over to the side you came from.
Sumo_Deadlift: Start with a loaded bar on the floor. Step up to it so that the bar runs over the middle of your feet. Place your feet very wide, close to the collars. Bend at the hips and grip the bar. Your arms hang straight below the shoulders, between your legs; a pronated grip, a mixed grip or a hook grip all work. Let your shoulders relax, which effectively makes your arms longer.
Breathe in, then drop your hips, eyes forward and chest up. Push into the floor and spread your feet apart, weight on the rear half of your feet. Straighten hips and knees.
Once the bar passes your knees, lean back, push your hips into the bar and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Bend at the hips to put the weight back on the floor, and keep it under control on the way down.
Sumo_Deadlift_with_Bands: Deadlifting with short bands is simple: before you start, loop them over the bar; to set up, step into them. They must be under the back half of your foot, directly where you drive into the floor.

Start with a loaded bar on the floor. Step up to it so that the bar runs over the middle of your feet. Place your feet very wide, close to the collars. Bend at the hips and grip the bar. Your arms hang straight below the shoulders, between your legs; a pronated grip, a mixed grip or a hook grip all work.
Breathe in, then drop your hips, eyes forward and chest up. Push into the floor and spread your feet apart, weight on the rear half of your feet. Straighten hips and knees.
Once the bar passes your knees, lean back, push your hips into the bar and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Bend at the hips to put the weight back on the floor, and keep it under control on the way down.
Sumo_Deadlift_with_Chains: Fasten the chains to the bar's sleeves, or simply hang their middle over the bar so that the weight grows more as you lift. Try to keep the chain ends clear of the plates so you do not hit them when the weight comes down.

Start with a loaded bar on the floor. Step up to it so that the bar runs over the middle of your feet. Place your feet very wide, close to the collars. Bend at the hips and grip the bar. Your arms hang straight below the shoulders, between your legs; a pronated grip, a mixed grip or a hook grip all work. Let your shoulders relax, which effectively makes your arms longer.
Breathe in, then drop your hips, eyes forward and chest up. Push into the floor and spread your feet apart, weight on the rear half of your feet. Straighten hips and knees.
Once the bar passes your knees, lean back, push your hips into the bar and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Bend at the hips to put the weight back on the floor, and keep it under control on the way down.
Superman: Lie stretched out, face down, on the floor or a mat, with your arms reaching straight out ahead of you. That is your starting position.

Lift arms, legs and chest off the floor at the same time and hold the contraction for 2 seconds. Tip: Tense your lower back for the best results. Do not forget to exhale as you lift. Note: In the held position you should look like Superman in flight.
Inhale and slowly bring arms, legs and chest down again to the starting position.
Do the number of repetitions your program prescribes.
Supine_Chest_Throw: This is a good drill for chest passes when you have no partner and no wall that is sturdy enough. Lie on your back on the floor and bend your knees.
Start with the ball resting on your chest, both hands holding it from below.
Push up explosively and straighten your elbows to throw the ball straight up above you, as high as you can.
When the ball comes down, catch it in both hands.
Supine_One-Arm_Overhead_Throw: Lie on your back on the floor and bend your knees. Take the ball in one hand and stretch that arm out fully behind your head. That is your starting position.
Start the movement from the shoulder: sit up and throw the ball straight ahead, aiming for as much distance as possible.
Throw the ball to a partner or let it bounce off a wall.
Supine_Two-Arm_Overhead_Throw: Lie on your back on the floor and bend your knees.
Take the ball in both hands and stretch your arms out fully behind your head. That is your starting position.
Start the movement from the shoulders: sit up and throw the ball straight ahead, aiming for as much distance as possible.
Throw the ball to a partner or let it bounce off a wall.
Suspended_Fallout: Set the straps so that the handles hang at a suitable height, lower than your waist.
Start standing, with the handles in your hands. Lean into the straps until you are in an incline push-up position. That is your starting position.
With straight arms, lean deeper into the suspension straps so your body comes nearer the floor. Let your shoulders open so that your arms rise up and over your head.
Keep your spine neutral and the rest of your body in a straight line; the shoulders are the only joints that may move.
Pause at the point of peak contraction, then go back to the starting position.
Suspended_Push-Up: The top of a rack or another object serves as the anchor; attach your suspension straps to it securely.

Lean into the straps, take one handle in each hand and get into a push-up plank position. With your arms fully extended and your posture good, your body should be as near to parallel with the floor as you can manage.
Keep your torso straight and rigid and lower yourself slowly by letting your elbows bend.
Go on until your elbows bend past 90 degrees. Pause, then straighten your arms to come back to the starting position.
Suspended_Reverse_Crunch: Fix a pair of suspension straps so the handles hang roughly a foot above the floor. Get into a push-up plank position with your back to the rack.
Put your feet in the handles. Hold your body straight and do not let your hips sag. That is your starting position.
Start by bending knees and hips and pulling your knees towards your torso. While doing so, tilt your pelvis anteriorly and let your spine round.
Once the controlled movement reaches its top, come back to where you started.
Suspended_Row: With the straps suspended at about chest height, take a handle in each hand. Lean back with fully extended arms, an erect body, and head and chest up. You are now in the starting position.
Start the movement by bending your elbows. Protract your shoulder blades while you do.
Pause when the movement is complete, then go back to the starting position.
Suspended_Split_Squat: The handles should be 18-30 inches from the floor; suspend your straps accordingly.
Stand with your back to the setup and put your rear foot into the handle behind you. Look straight ahead, lift your chest and bend your knee slightly. That is your starting position.
Bend knee and hips to lower yourself towards the floor. Keep your weight on your heel and hold your posture for the whole exercise.
At the bottom, change direction: straighten hip and knee to come back to the starting position.
Svend_Press: Squeeze two light plates together between your hands. Hold them pressed together close to your chest, so your chest muscles contract isometrically. Your fingers point forward. That is your starting position.
Keep pressing the plates between your palms and push your arms straight out in front of you with control.
At the top of the movement, pause; go slowly back to where you started.
T-Bar_Row_with_Handle: Put one end of a bar into a landmine or a corner so it cannot move. Load a suitable weight onto the free end.
Straddle the bar and place a double-D row handle around it, next to the collar. Stand up using your hips and legs.
Take a wide stance, hips back and chest up, arms extended. That is your starting position.
Draw your shoulder blades back and bend your elbows to pull the weight to your upper abdomen. Do not jerk the weight and do not cheat.
Pause briefly, then go back to the starting position.
Tate_Press: Lie on a flat bench, a dumbbell in each hand resting on your thighs, palms turned towards each other.

With the help of your thighs, bring the dumbbells up one arm at a time until you hold them in front of you at shoulder width. Note: While holding the dumbbells in front of you, your arms must be wider than shoulder width apart, in a pronated grip with palms forward. Let your elbows point outward. That is your starting position.

Hold your upper arms still, inhale and slowly move the dumbbells inward and down in a half circle until they touch your upper chest. Stay in full control of the dumbbells throughout; do not move your upper arms and do not rest the dumbbells on your chest.

Exhale and press the dumbbells up with your triceps, along the same half circle in reverse. Try to keep the dumbbells together on the way up. Lock your arms in the contracted position, hold for a second, then slowly start down again. Tip: Lowering should take at least twice as long as lifting.
Repeat for the number of repetitions your training program prescribes.
The_Straddle: Sit upright. Stretch your legs out in front of you in a V shape.
Put your hands on the floor and lean as far forward as you can. Hold for 10 to 20 seconds.
Thigh_Abductor: Sit in the abductor machine and choose a weight you feel comfortable with. Once your legs are in the right place, take hold of the handles on both sides. Everything from the waist up stays still. That is your starting position.
Exhale and slowly push your legs against the machine so that they move apart.
Feel the contraction for a second, then inhale and bring your legs back to the starting position. Note: Keep your upper body still so that you do not injure yourself.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Thigh_Adductor: Sit in the adductor machine and choose a weight you feel comfortable with. Once your legs sit correctly against the machine's leg pads, take hold of the handles on both sides. Everything from the waist up stays still. That is your starting position.
Exhale and slowly push your legs against the machine so that they move together.
Feel the contraction for a second, then inhale and bring your legs back to the starting position. Note: Keep your upper body still and avoid fast, jerky movements so that you do not injure yourself.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Tire_Flip: Grab the tire at the bottom, on the tread, and set your feet a little way back. Press your chest into the tire.
Lift the tire by straightening hips, knees and ankles, pushing into the tire and upward.

When the tire is at a 45 degree angle, step forward and drive one knee into it. At the same time move your hands to the upper part of the tire and shove it forward as hard as you can to finish the flip. Repeat as often as needed.
Toe_Touchers: Lie on the floor or a mat with your back pressed flat against the floor. Rest your arms at your sides, palms down.
Keep your legs touching. Slowly lift them until they are nearly vertical to the floor, knees slightly bent. The soles of your feet are parallel to the floor.
Stretch your arms out fully at a 45 degree angle to the floor. That is your starting position.
With your lower back still pressed to the floor, slowly raise your torso and try to reach your toes with your hands. Do not forget to exhale during this part.
Inhale and slowly bring your torso and arms back down to the starting position. Keep your arms straight and pointing at your toes.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Torso_Rotation: Stand upright with an exercise ball in both hands. Stretch your arms so that you hold the ball straight out ahead of you. That is your starting position.
Turn your torso to one side and follow the ball with your eyes as you move. Then turn back the other way. Do 10-20 repetitions.
Trail_Running_Walking: Running or hiking on trails gets your blood flowing and your heart working almost at once. Wear good shoes. Going uphill, your calves and glutes pull you up; coming down, your knees, joints and ankles take most of the pounding. Walk downhill with shorter steps, keep your knees bent to soften the impact, and slow down so you do not fall.
Walking uphill for 30 minutes, someone weighing 150 lb can burn more than 200 calories, against 175 on flat ground. Running the trail, a 150 lb person can burn well above 500 calories in 30 minutes.
Trap_Bar_Deadlift: Load a trap bar, also called a hex bar, with a suitable weight and leave it on the floor. Step into the middle of the bar and take hold of both handles.
Drop your hips, look straight ahead and lift your chest.
Start by pushing through your heels and straightening hips and knees. Never let your back round.
When the lift is complete, lower the weight to the floor with control.
Tricep_Dumbbell_Kickback: Hold a dumbbell in each hand, palms turned towards your torso. With a straight back and slightly bent knees, lean forward from the waist until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your head up. Hold your upper arms close to your torso and parallel to the floor, and let your forearms point down at the floor with the weights. Forearm and upper arm form a 90-degree angle. That is your starting position.
Hold your upper arms still, exhale and use your triceps to raise the weights until your arms are fully extended. Concentrate on moving only the forearm.
Pause briefly at the top contraction. Then breathe in while the dumbbells come slowly back down to where you started.
Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions.
Tricep_Side_Stretch: Take your right arm across your body and over your left shoulder. Hold the elbow with your left hand until your triceps stretches. Then do the same with the other arm.
Triceps_Overhead_Extension_with_Rope: Fasten a rope to a low pulley. Choose a suitable weight, take the rope in both hands and turn your back to the cable.

Bring your hands behind your head, elbows pointing straight up. Your elbows are bent at the start. For more stability, you can stand in a staggered stance and lean slightly away from the machine. That is your starting position.
Straighten your elbows and raise your hands above your head, keeping your upper arms where they are.
At the top, squeeze your triceps, then slowly lower the weight to the starting position.
Triceps_Pushdown: Fasten a straight or angled bar to a high pulley and grip it at shoulder width with an overhand grip, palms down.

Stand upright, torso straight and leaning forward only very slightly. Bring your upper arms close to your body, vertical to the floor. Your forearms point up at the pulley while they hold the bar. That is your starting position.

Use your triceps to press the bar down until it touches the front of your thighs and your arms are fully extended, vertical to the floor. Your upper arms stay fixed beside your torso the whole time; the forearms alone move. Exhale during this movement.
Hold the contracted position for a second, then let the bar rise slowly to the starting point. Inhale during this part.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Triceps_Pushdown_-_Rope_Attachment: Fasten a rope to a high pulley and take it with a neutral grip, palms turned towards each other.

Stand upright, torso straight and leaning forward only very slightly. Bring your upper arms close to your body, vertical to the floor. Your forearms point up at the pulley while they hold the rope, palms towards each other. That is your starting position.

Use your triceps to press the rope down, guiding each end of it to the side of your thighs. At the end your arms are fully extended and vertical to the floor. Your upper arms stay fixed beside your torso the whole time; the forearms alone move. Exhale during this movement.
Hold the contracted position for a second, then let the rope rise slowly to the starting point. Inhale during this part.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Triceps_Pushdown_-_V-Bar_Attachment: Fix a V-bar to the high pulley. Take it at shoulder width with your palms turned down (overhand grip).

Stand tall with a straight torso that leans forward only a touch. Tuck your upper arms in against your body so they are perpendicular to the floor. Your forearms hold the bar and point up at the pulley, with your thumbs sitting higher than your little fingers. This is the starting position.

Press the bar down with your triceps until it meets the front of your thighs and your arms are completely straight and perpendicular to the floor. Your upper arms stay fixed beside your torso the whole time; nothing but the forearms moves. Breathe out during this phase.
Hold the contraction for a second, then let the V-bar rise slowly to where you started. Breathe in on the way up.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Triceps_Stretch: Bring one hand behind your head, take hold of that elbow with the other hand and pull it gently. Stay there for 10 to 20 seconds, then do the other side.
Tuck_Crunch: Lie on the floor or on an exercise mat and press your back flat into it. Rest your arms along your sides, palms turned down.

Cross your legs by hooking one ankle around the other. Raise them slowly into the air until your thighs are perpendicular to the floor, knees slightly bent. Note: It is your knees and toes that run parallel to the floor, not your thighs.
Take your arms off the floor and fold them over your chest so they rest there. This is the starting position.
With your lower back still pressed into the floor, raise your torso slowly. Breathe out during this part of the exercise.
Breathe in and slowly let your torso sink back to the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Two-Arm_Dumbbell_Preacher_Curl: Take a dumbbell in each hand and lay your upper arms on the pad of a preacher bench or on an incline bench. Hold the dumbbells at shoulder length. This is the starting position.
Breathe in and slowly let the dumbbells down until your upper arms are extended and your biceps are stretched all the way.
Breathe out and curl the weights up with your biceps until the muscle is completely contracted and the dumbbells have reached shoulder height.
At the top, squeeze your biceps hard for a second. Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Two-Arm_Kettlebell_Clean: Set two kettlebells down between your feet. For the starting position, send your hips backward and keep your eyes straight ahead.
Clean the kettlebells: straighten your legs and hips while you bring the kettlebells up to your shoulders, turning your wrists on the way.
Let the kettlebells come down to where you started, then do it again.
Two-Arm_Kettlebell_Jerk: Bring two kettlebells to your shoulders with a clean: straighten your legs and hips while the kettlebells swing up to your shoulders, and turn your wrists on the way until your palms point forward. Dip into a squat of a few inches, then quickly reverse and drive both kettlebells overhead. Right after that first push, drop into a squat once more to get beneath the kettlebells. When your arms are locked out, stand up straight to finish the exercise.
Two-Arm_Kettlebell_Military_Press: Bring two kettlebells to your shoulders with a clean: straighten your legs and hips while the kettlebells swing up to your shoulders, and turn your wrists on the way until your palms point forward.
Push the kettlebells upward and outward. Once they are past your head, lean in toward the weights so they end up racked behind your head. Tighten your lats, glutes and stomach to stay more stable.
Two-Arm_Kettlebell_Row: Set two kettlebells down in front of your feet. With a slight bend in your knees, send your hips back as far as you can while you lean over into the starting position.
Take hold of both kettlebells and row them to your stomach by bending your elbows and drawing your shoulder blades back. Your back stays straight. Let the weights down and repeat.
Underhand_Cable_Pulldowns: Take a seat at a pulldown machine that has a wide bar on the top pulley. Set the knee pad to suit your height. The pads keep the resistance on the bar from lifting your body.
Take the pulldown bar with a supinated grip, palms turned toward your torso. Your hands should be closer together than shoulder width.

With both arms stretched out in front of you and the bar held at that grip width, lean your torso back by roughly 30 degrees, arch your lower back and push your chest out. This is the starting position.

Breathe out and draw your shoulders and upper arms down and back so the bar comes down to touch your upper chest. Tip: When you reach full contraction, focus on squeezing your back muscles, and keep your elbows close to your body. Your upper torso stays still while the bar comes toward you; only your arms move. Your forearms have no job except holding the bar.
Stay contracted for a second, then breathe in and slowly let the bar return to the starting position, where your arms are completely straight and your lats fully stretched.
Do the number of repetitions your plan prescribes.
Upper_Back-Leg_Grab: Sit down and lean forward so you can wrap both arms around your thighs from below.
With your knees together and your legs stretched out, lower your chest to your knees. To stretch the middle back as well, pull your back away from your knees while you keep hugging them.
Upper_Back_Stretch: Interlock your fingers with the thumbs pointing downward, then reach your hands forward and let your shoulders round.
Upright_Barbell_Row: Take a barbell with an overhand grip a little narrower than shoulder width. Let it rest on the top of your thighs, arms extended with the elbows slightly bent. Keep your back straight too. This is the starting position.

Breathe out and lift the bar with the sides of your shoulders, bringing your elbows up and out to the side. The bar stays close to your body on the way up. Keep lifting until it almost touches your chin. Tip: Let your elbows lead the movement and keep them higher than your forearms at all times. Hold your torso still and pause for a second at the top.
Slowly let the bar down to the starting position. Breathe in during this part of the movement.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Upright_Cable_Row: Attach a straight bar to a low pulley and take it with a pronated grip (palms toward your thighs) a little narrower than shoulder width. Let the bar rest on the top of your thighs. Extend your arms with the elbows slightly bent and keep your back straight. This is the starting position.

Breathe out and lift the bar with the sides of your shoulders. Keep it close to your body on the way up. Keep lifting until it almost touches your chin. Tip: Let your elbows lead the movement. While the bar rises, they stay higher than your forearms at all times. Hold your torso still as well, and pause for a second at the top.
Slowly let the bar down to the starting position. Breathe in during this part of the movement.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Upright_Row_-_With_Bands: Stand on an exercise band in such a way that it starts to pull when your arms hang at full length. Take the handles with a pronated grip (palms toward your thighs) a little narrower than shoulder width. Let the handles rest on the top of your thighs. Extend your arms with the elbows slightly bent and keep your back straight. This is the starting position.

Breathe out and lift the handles with the sides of your shoulders. Keep them close to your body on the way up. Keep lifting until they almost touch your chin. Tip: Let your elbows lead the movement. While the handles rise, your elbows stay higher than your forearms at all times. Hold your torso still as well, and pause for a second at the top.
Slowly let the handles down to the starting position. Breathe in during this part of the movement.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Upward_Stretch: Stretch both arms straight up over your head with your palms pressed together.
Keep your back straight and slowly press your hands upward and backward.
V-Bar_Pulldown: Take a seat at a pulldown machine that has a V-bar on the top pulley.
Set the knee pad to suit your height. The pads keep the resistance on the bar from lifting your body.
Take the V-bar with a neutral grip, palms turned toward each other. Push your chest out and lean back a little (about 30 degrees) so your lats work better. This is the starting position.

Pull the bar down with your lats and squeeze your shoulder blades as you do. Keep going until the V-bar is almost at your chest. Breathe out during this motion. Tip: Your torso stays still for the whole movement.
Hold the contraction for a second, then breathe in and slowly let the bar return to the starting position.
Do the number of repetitions your plan prescribes.
V-Bar_Pullup: Lay the middle of the V-bar over the middle of the pull-up bar (this assumes your pull-up station has no neutral-grip handles). The handles of the V-bar point down, so you can hang from the pull-up bar by them.
When the V-bar sits securely, take a handle on each side and hang from it. Push your chest out and lean back a little so your lats work better. This is the starting position.
Pull your torso up with your lats, tilting your head back a little so the pull-up bar does not hit you. Keep going until your chest is almost at the V-bar. Breathe out during this motion.
Hold the contraction for a second, then breathe in and slowly let your body down to the starting position.
Do the number of repetitions your plan prescribes.
Vertical_Swing: Hold one dumbbell in both hands and let it hang between your legs with your arms long. Your back is straight and your head is up.
Swing the dumbbell back between your legs by hinging at the hips with a slight bend in your knees.
Reverse the motion with power: extend your hips, knees and ankles to launch yourself upward and swing the dumbbell over your head.
On landing, let your legs take up the impact and pull the dumbbell in to your torso before you start the next repetition.
Walking_Treadmill: Step onto the treadmill and choose the option you want from the menu. On most treadmills you can pick a manual setting or run a program. Usually you can type in your age and weight for an estimate of the calories you burn while exercising. Change the elevation to make the workout more or less intense.

A treadmill is convenient, trains your cardiovascular system and is usually lower in impact than walking outdoors. Walk at a moderate to fast pace rather than strolling. Because walking is a lower-intensity activity, it burns fewer calories than some other activities, yet it is still very beneficial. A person of 150 lb burns roughly 175 calories in 30 minutes of walking at 4 miles per hour; running twice as fast burns 450 calories. Keep a proper posture while you walk and hold the handles only when you need to, for example when you get off or check your heart rate.
Weighted_Ball_Hyperextension: Lie face down over an exercise ball so that your torso presses into the ball and is parallel to the floor. Press the balls of your feet into the floor to help you keep your balance. Hold a weight plate under your chin or behind your neck. This is the starting position.
Bend at the lower back and waist to bring your torso up slowly. Remember: breathe out as you do this.
For a second, keep the contraction on your lower back. Then inhale while your torso goes back down to where you started.
Do as many repetitions as your program prescribes.
Weighted_Ball_Side_Bend: Lie on an exercise ball with the left side of your torso (waist, hip and shoulder) pressed into it.

Keep your feet on the floor with your legs crossed and hanging off the ball. In your right hand, hold a weight plate right next to the right side of your head. Tip: The smooth side of the plate should rest against your head.
Lay your left arm across your torso with the palm on your obliques. Your left forearm and upper arm form a right angle. This is the starting position.
Breathe out and lift the side of your torso by bending sideways at the waist.
Hold the contraction for a second, then breathe in and slowly sink back to the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Change sides and do the exercise again.
Weighted_Bench_Dip: You need two benches for this exercise: one behind your back and one in front of you. Both stand perpendicular to your body. Grip the edge of the bench behind you with your hands near your body, shoulder width apart, and your arms completely straight.

Stretch your legs forward and rest them on the other bench. Your legs are parallel to the floor and your torso is perpendicular to it. Let your partner put the dumbbell on your lap. Note: It is best to do this exercise with a partner, because getting the weight onto your lap alone can be difficult and can lead to injury. This is the starting position.

Breathe in and slowly sink down by bending your elbows, until the angle between upper arm and forearm is a little under 90 degrees. Tip: Keep your elbows as close in as you can throughout. Your forearms point down at all times.
Breathe out and push your torso up with your triceps until you are back in the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Weighted_Crunches: Get flat onto your back. Your knees are bent to 90 degrees, and your feet either rest on a bench or stand flat on the ground.
The weight is held to your chest, or you may extend it above your torso. That is the starting position.
Breathe out and slowly curl your shoulders up from the floor. They should rise about 4 inches, while your lower back stays down.
At the top, tense your abdominals and pause briefly.
Breathe in and slowly return to the starting position.
Weighted_Jump_Squat: Across the back of your shoulders, place a barbell with a light load. For this exercise, other types of resistance, such as a sandbag or a weighted vest, could be used as well.
Pick a weight light enough not to slow you down noticeably. Stand with your feet just wider than shoulder width, head and chest up. This is the starting position.
Dip into a partial squat as a countermovement, then reverse at once and explode off the ground by extending your hips, knees and ankles. Keep a good posture through the whole jump.
When you come down, let your legs take up the impact.
Weighted_Pull_Ups: Hang a weight from a dip belt and fasten the belt around your waist. Take the pull-up bar with your palms facing forward. Shoulder-width spacing of the hands gives you a medium grip. Hold the bar at your chosen grip with both arms extended in front of you.
Lean your torso back by about 30 degrees, arch your lower back and push your chest out. This is the starting position.
Breathe out and pull your torso up until your head is higher than your hands. As you arrive at the top, focus on squeezing your shoulder blades back and down.
Stay at the top for a brief moment, then breathe in and slowly let your torso down to the starting position, arms extended and lats fully stretched.
Weighted_Sissy_Squat: Stand upright with your feet shoulder width apart and your toes raised. Hold on to the beam of a squat rack with one hand, and with the other arm hold a plate against the top of your chest. This is the starting position.

Supporting yourself with the one arm, bend your knees and slowly lower your torso toward the ground by pushing your pelvis and knees forward. Breathe in on the way down and stop when your upper and lower legs form almost a 90-degree angle. Stay in the stretched position for a second.
Once the one second hold is over, bring your torso back up to the starting position with your thigh muscles, exhaling on the way up.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Weighted_Sit-Ups_-_With_Bands: Loop the bands around the base of the decline bench. Lay the handles toward the inside of the bench so you can reach both of them once you are lying down.

Slide your legs into the decline bench until they are held securely. Then reach for the bands with both hands and take the handles with a pronated grip (palms forward). Bring them close to your collarbone and turn your wrists into a neutral grip (palms toward your torso). Note: Your arms do not move during the whole exercise. This is the starting position.
Breathe out and raise your torso until your upper body is perpendicular to the floor. Hold the contraction for a second, then breathe in and lower your upper body to the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Weighted_Squat: Place two flat benches shoulder width apart. Stand on them and fasten the weight belt around your waist, loaded with a weight you are comfortable with. Your toes should point outward.
Stand straight up with the weight hanging in between your legs. Then extend your arms fully at the side of your body. That is the starting position.

Bend your knees while you keep an upright posture with your head up. Go down until the angle between your thighs and calves is a little under 90 degrees (at that point your thighs are below parallel to the floor). Breathe in during this part of the movement. Tip: Done correctly, the front of your knees forms an imaginary straight line with your toes, perpendicular to the front. If your knees go beyond that line (past your toes), you put undue stress on the knee and the exercise is not done correctly.

Come back up by pressing into the surface of the bench, mostly with the balls of your feet, while you straighten your legs and return to the starting position. Breathe out during this part of the exercise.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Wide-Grip_Barbell_Bench_Press: Lie on a flat bench and plant your feet firmly on the floor. Take the bar with a wide pronated grip (palms forward), each hand about 3 inches outside shoulder width. Lift it out of the rack and hold it straight above you with locked arms. The bar is perpendicular to your torso and to the floor. This is the starting position.
Breathe in and lower the bar slowly until you feel it on the middle of your chest.

Pause for a second, then breathe out and press the bar back to the starting position with your chest muscles. Lock your arms, squeeze your chest in the contracted position for a second, and then begin to lower slowly again. Tip: Lowering should take at least twice as long as pressing up.
Do the number of repetitions your plan prescribes.
Wide-Grip_Decline_Barbell_Bench_Press: Lie on a decline bench with your feet locked securely at the front of the bench. Take the bar with a wide pronated grip (palms forward), each hand about 3 inches outside shoulder width. Lift it out of the rack and hold it straight above you with locked arms. The bar is perpendicular to your torso and to the floor. This is the starting position.
Breathe in and lower the bar slowly until you feel it on your lower chest.

Pause for a second, then breathe out and press the bar back to the starting position with your chest muscles. Lock your arms, squeeze your chest in the contracted position for a second, and then begin to lower slowly again. Tip: Lowering should take at least twice as long as pressing up.
Do the number of repetitions your plan prescribes.
Wide-Grip_Decline_Barbell_Pullover: Lie on a decline bench with both legs locked securely in place. Reach behind your head for the barbell and take it with a pronated grip (palms facing out). For this exercise, grip the bar wider than shoulder width. Slowly raise the barbell off the floor with your arms.
In the right position your arms are completely straight and perpendicular to the floor. This is the starting position.

Move the barbell back down in a half circle as though you meant to put it on the floor, but stop once your arms are parallel to the floor. Tip: Keep your arms completely straight the whole time. Only the shoulder joint should move. Breathe in during this part of the movement.
Breathe out and bring the barbell up until you are in the starting position again. Stay in full control of the barbell throughout.
Do the number of repetitions your training program prescribes.
At the end of the set, slowly lower the barbell until it is level with your head, then let go of it.
Wide-Grip_Lat_Pulldown: Take a seat at a pulldown machine that has a wide bar on the top pulley. Set the knee pad to suit your height. The pads keep the resistance on the bar from lifting your body.

Take the bar with your palms facing forward, using the grip your plan prescribes. Note on grips: A wide grip means your hands are further apart than shoulder width. A medium grip means they are exactly shoulder width apart, and a close grip means they are less than shoulder width apart.

With both arms stretched out in front of you and the bar held at that grip width, lean your torso back by roughly 30 degrees, arch your lower back and push your chest out. This is the starting position.

Breathe out and draw your shoulders and upper arms down and back so the bar comes down to touch your upper chest. Tip: When you reach full contraction, focus on squeezing your back muscles. Your upper torso stays still and only your arms move. Your forearms have no job except holding the bar, so do not try to pull the bar down with them.

Squeeze your shoulder blades together in the contracted position for a second, then slowly let the bar rise to the starting position, where your arms are completely straight and your lats fully stretched. Breathe in during this part of the movement.
Do the number of repetitions your plan prescribes.
Wide-Grip_Pulldown_Behind_The_Neck: Fix a wide bar to the high pulley of a pulldown station and take a seat. Set the knee pad to suit your height. The pad keeps the load on the bar from lifting you off the seat.

Take the bar with your palms turned forward, at the grip width you were given. Note: A wide grip means hands further apart than your shoulders. A medium grip means hands as far apart as your shoulders, and a close grip means hands nearer together than that.

With both arms stretched out and your hands on the bar at the width you chose, lean your torso and head forward. Picture a line running from the middle of the bar to the back of your neck. You are now in the starting position.

Breathe out and pull the bar down, moving your shoulders and upper arms down and back, until the bar touches the back of your neck. Tip: Once the bar is all the way down, focus on squeezing your back muscles. Keep your upper body still and let only your arms move. Your forearms are there to hold the bar and nothing more, so do not pull with them.

Stay there for a second with your shoulder blades pressed together. Then let the bar rise slowly, breathing in, until your arms are straight and your lats are fully stretched in the starting position.
Do the movement again for as many repetitions as prescribed.
Wide-Grip_Rear_Pull-Up: Take a wide grip on the pull-up bar, palms turned forward.
Hang with both arms stretched out and move your torso and head forward, so that you can picture a line from the bar to the back of your neck. You are now in the starting position.

Raise your body until the back of your neck is close to the bar. Do it by moving your shoulders and upper arms down and back, with your head tilted a little forward. Breathe out during this part. Tip: Once you are all the way up, focus on squeezing your back muscles. Keep your upper body rigid while it travels, and let only your arms move. Your forearms hold the bar and do nothing else.
Stay at the top for a second. Then begin to breathe in and come down slowly until your arms are straight and your lats are fully stretched in the starting position.
Do the movement again for as many repetitions as prescribed.
Wide-Grip_Standing_Barbell_Curl: Stand tall with an upright torso and take the barbell by its wide outer grip section. Turn your palms forward. Keep your elbows near your sides. You are now in the starting position.
Keep your upper arms still, breathe out, and bring the bar up in front of you by tightening your biceps. Tip: Nothing but your forearms should move.
Go on until the bar reaches shoulder height and your biceps are tightened all the way. Stay there for a second and squeeze your biceps firmly.
Breathe in and let the bar come down slowly to where you started.
Do as many repetitions as recommended.
Wide_Stance_Barbell_Squat: For safety, do this exercise inside a squat rack. Set the bar in the rack at the height that suits you best. With the height right and the bar loaded, step under it and lay it across the back of your shoulders, a little below the neck.
Hold the bar with both hands, one on each side, and lift it out of the rack by pushing with your legs while you straighten your torso.

Step back from the rack and set your feet wider than shoulder width, toes turned out slightly. Keep your head up the whole time, because looking down throws you off balance, and keep your back straight. This is the starting position.

Slowly lower the bar by bending your knees while you keep an upright posture with your head up. Go down until the angle between your thighs and calves is a little under 90 degrees (at that point your thighs are below parallel to the floor). Breathe in during this part of the movement. Tip: Done correctly, the front of your knees forms an imaginary straight line with your toes, perpendicular to the front. If your knees go beyond that line (past your toes), you put undue stress on the knee and the exercise is not done correctly.
Breathe out and raise the bar by pressing your heels into the floor while you straighten your legs and return to the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your plan calls for.
Wide_Stance_Stiff_Legs: Start with a loaded barbell lying on the floor. Take a wide stance and hinge at the hips to grip the bar. Push your hips back as far as they go and keep your legs almost straight. Your back is straight, your head and chest are up. This is the starting position.

Start the lift from your hips: drive them forward and let your arms hang straight. Keep going until you stand fully upright, then slowly bring the weight back to the starting position. On the following reps the weight does not have to touch the floor.
Wind_Sprints: Take an overhand grip on a pull-up bar and hang from it. Keep both arms and both legs straight. You are now in the starting position.
Start by driving one knee up fast, as high as it will go. Keep your body and legs from swinging.
Bring that leg straight back down to the starting position without a pause. At the same moment, drive the other knee up as high as you can.
Keep switching legs until you have finished the set.
Windmills: Lie face up with your legs straight and your arms stretched out to both sides. You are now in the starting position.
Raise one leg and swing it quickly across your body. Try to tap the floor close to the hand on the other side.
Come back to where you started and do the same with the other leg. Keep switching sides for 10-20 repetitions.
Worlds_Greatest_Stretch: This stretch has three parts. Start with a lunge forward: the whole front foot rests on the floor and the back foot is up on its toes. Bend both knees and sink down until the back knee nearly touches the floor. Keep your torso upright and stay there for 10-20 seconds.

Next, bring the arm on the side of your front leg down to the floor, with the elbow beside the foot. Set your other hand on the floor, in line with your front leg, so that it supports you during this part of the stretch.

When 10-20 seconds have passed, put one hand on each side of your front foot. Lift the toes of that foot from the floor and straighten the leg. You may have to move your back leg to manage this. Stay for 10-20 seconds, then go through the whole sequence again on the other side.
Wrist_Circles: Stand upright with your feet as far apart as your shoulders. Lift your arms out to both sides until they are straight, level with your shoulders and parallel to the floor. Tip: Your torso and arms should make the shape of a "T". Turn your palms down. You are now in the starting position.
Hold the rest of your body still and move only your wrists: turn both of them forward in circles. Tip: Imagine painting circles with your hands as the brush. Breathe normally throughout the exercise.
Do as many repetitions as recommended.
Wrist_Roller: Start upright with a wrist roller in an overhand grip, palms turned down. Place your feet as far apart as your shoulders.

Raise both arms slowly in front of you until they are straight and parallel to the floor. Note: Check that the rope is not wound around the roller. Apart from your forearms, your whole body stays still. You are now in the starting position.
Turn your wrists upward, one after the other, so that the rope winds around the roller and the weight climbs up to the bar.
When the weight is at the bar, turn your wrists downward and let the weight sink slowly until it is back in the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as your program prescribes.
Wrist_Rotations_with_Straight_Bar: Take a barbell in both hands, palms turned down and hands roughly as far apart as your shoulders. You are now in the starting position.
Extend one wrist and then the other, as if you were rolling up a newspaper. Keep going from hand to hand until you cannot do any more.
Now go the other way: flex your wrists and roll in the opposite direction. Keep switching hands until you cannot do any more.
Yoke_Walk: A yoke frame is the usual tool for this exercise, though some people carry a refrigerator or another heavy object instead.
Start by setting the frame across the back of your shoulders. Look straight ahead, arch your back and push through your heels to lift the yoke.
Walk off as fast as you can with short, rapid steps. You may grip the side posts of the yoke to steady it and keep it in place. Cover the set distance, usually 75-100 feet, as fast as you can.
Zercher_Squats: For safety, do this exercise inside a squat rack if you can. Start by placing the bar in the rack at the height that suits you best: somewhere above your waist and below your chest. When the height is right and the weight is on the bar, clasp your hands together and take the bar into the crook of your arms, between forearm and upper arm.
Raise the bar so that your forearms carry it. Held correctly, it looks as though your arms were crossed with a bar lying across them.

Move away from the rack and stand with your feet shoulder width apart in a medium stance, toes turned out a little. Keep your head up the whole time, because looking down throws you off balance, and keep your back straight. You are now in the starting position. Note: The medium stance described here trains the legs as a whole, but you can use any of the three stances.

Bend your knees to bring the bar down, staying upright with your head up. Go on until your upper legs and calves form an angle of slightly less than 90 degrees, which is where your upper legs are below parallel to the floor. Breathe in during this part. Tip: Done correctly, the front of your knees and your toes lie on one imaginary straight line that is perpendicular to the front. If your knees go beyond that line, that is past your toes, you are loading the knee too much and the exercise is done wrongly.
Breathe out and bring the bar up again: press into the floor, mostly with the balls of your feet, and straighten your legs until you are back in the starting position.
Do as many repetitions as recommended.
Zottman_Curl: Stand tall with an upright torso, a dumbbell in each hand and your arms hanging straight. Keep your elbows near your sides.
Check that your palms are turned toward each other. You are now in the starting position.

Keep your upper arms still, breathe out and bring the dumbbells up by tightening your biceps. Nothing but your forearms should move. Turn your wrists on the way so that you end in a supinated grip, palms up. Go on until the dumbbells reach shoulder height and your biceps are tightened all the way.
Stay at the top for a second and squeeze your biceps.
Still at the top, turn your wrists into a pronated grip, palms down, with your thumbs higher than your little fingers.
Let the dumbbells come down slowly in this pronated grip.
When the dumbbells get near your thighs, begin to turn your wrists back into a neutral grip, palms toward your body.
Do as many repetitions as recommended.
Zottman_Preacher_Curl: Take a dumbbell in each hand and rest your upper arms on the pad of a preacher bench or an incline bench. Bend your elbows and hold the dumbbells at shoulder height. Turn your palms down. You are now in the starting position.
Breathe in and let the dumbbells sink slowly, palms still down, until your arms are straight and your biceps are fully stretched.
At the bottom of the movement, turn your wrists so that your palms point up.

Breathe out and bring the dumbbells up with your biceps until the muscles are tightened all the way and the weights are at shoulder height. Keep in mind once more that a full contraction needs your little finger higher than your thumb.
Squeeze your biceps firmly at the top for a second, then turn your wrists until your palms point down again.
Do as many repetitions as recommended.
